contributions.summary: Builds a mechanism-first decomposition chain from enzyme-substrate reaction through Michaelis-Menten kinetics, enzyme deactivation, and analytic concentration relations.
Attempts to insert the official growth/moisture trait trade-off into the kinetic coefficient used by multiple-fungus scenarios.
Separates complementarity and shared-resource competition through two substrate-specific pair narratives.
Uses a Logistic baseline and two-population competition equations to give short/long interaction stories.
Presents aligned three-pair small multiples for resource-rich and resource-limited horizons.
Makes the environment-to-growth-to-interaction interface explicit and repeats the same scenario layout for two pairs.
Uses mediator-chain diagrams and matched single/pair plots to translate environment into decomposition.
Combines a representative-value map with matched temperature and humidity decision tables.
Returns species-level trait trade-offs to a functional-diversity and resilience narrative.
Fulfills the two-page audience artifact with layered definitions, examples, horizon explanations, and ecosystem context.

data_and_preprocessing.summary: The paper uses a small moisture-tolerance/decomposition scatter, but does not name the records, sample provenance, coefficient table, residuals, or uncertainty.
Three species I_c values are derived from looked-up growth rates; exact growth values, units, citations, and the intermediate m=g(u) relation are absent.
All species share 0.15 g initial and 0.5 g maximum dry weight; these common values make scenarios comparable but are not sourced.
Growth rates 0.05, 0.025, and 0.075 enter population trajectories without a printed unit or source.
Temperature ranges 30-35, 25-30, and 20-25 C plus humidity 95, 85, and 75 percent parameterize environmental response, but later prose conflicts with these values.
Washington, Sahara, Gansu, and Congo Basin labels supply selected temperature or humidity inputs without source, averaging period, or spatial uncertainty.
The table reports roughly 5 percent at 7 C and specific percentages at 23 and 30 C, but no time horizon or reproducible calculation is supplied.
The table reports near-zero, semi-arid, and rainforest percentages from humidity categories, but range-to-point selection and calculation are missing.

edges.handoff: The reaction participants and catalytic sequence motivate the Michaelis-Menten substrate-rate law.
r_c becomes the negative substrate derivative dC/dt.
The first-order deactivation law becomes dE/dt and supplies k_d.
The solved concentration relation supplies the single-species decomposition trajectory.
The two-trait functional interface is reduced to the paper's linear competitiveness formula.
Species I_c values replace the kinetic inactivation coefficient in single and pair scenarios.
The one-species Logistic state and capacity receive cross-population competition terms.
The independent Logistic baseline is evaluated over the seven-day resource-rich horizon.
The competition ODEs are evaluated over the declared long-term horizon.
Temperature-specific growth rates replace r_1 and r_2 in the pair system.
Temperature-conditioned population growth is propagated through competitiveness to decomposition.
The single and pair decomposition framework receives temperature-adjusted growth.
The same decomposition framework receives humidity-mediated growth and competitiveness.
Qualitative atmospheric consequences motivate the region and environmental scenario classes.
Temperature decomposition curves provide values and rankings for temperate and tropical rows.
Humidity decomposition curves provide values and rankings for arid, semi-arid, and rainforest rows.
Environment-specific turnover among advantaged species supplies the qualitative functional-diversity argument.

independent_extensions.summary: Replace the k_d/I_c substitution with a dimensionally typed mapping k_d=k_base+h(u,m) calibrated from enzyme-activity data.
Fit the official growth/decomposition and moisture-trade-off relations jointly with uncertainty, residual diagnostics, and an independent holdout.
Calibrate direction-specific competition coefficients from pair culture data rather than choosing them from desired coexistence classes.
Use a smooth species-specific thermal performance curve and a separate ambient-humidity response, with uncertainty on thresholds and optima.
Propagate temperature and humidity through both fungal growth and enzyme kinetics, preserving units and covariance.
Model all official environments, including arboreal conditions, with distributions rather than one representative point.
Define persistence, decomposition efficiency, diversity, and resilience metrics before ranking ecological outcomes.
Simulate communities larger than pairs with an interaction matrix and richness/composition-controlled comparisons.
Publish code, parameter provenance, time horizons, solver settings, and automated equation-figure-table parity tests.
Validate trajectories and regional rankings against independent decomposition or community-composition observations.

models.summary: MU-A-2021-2110178-001: Represent the chemical sequence underlying fungal decomposition. Inputs: A, E_0. Outputs: P, E_0.
MU-A-2021-2110178-002: Compute instantaneous substrate decomposition rate from active enzyme and substrate concentrations. Inputs: V_E, E, C, K_m. Outputs: r_c.
MU-A-2021-2110178-003: Represent time-dependent loss of extracellular-enzyme activity. Inputs: k_d, E. Outputs: r_E.
MU-A-2021-2110178-004: Solve active-enzyme decay and substrate depletion through time. Inputs: t, k_d, K_m, V_E, a, P_0, C_0. Outputs: E, C.
MU-A-2021-2110178-005: Represent interaction-driven enzyme inactivation with growth and moisture traits. Inputs: u, m. Outputs: I_c.
MU-A-2021-2110178-006: Assign one competitiveness value to each of the three fungi from extension rate. Inputs: u. Outputs: I_c.
MU-A-2021-2110178-007: Compare cellulose and lignin decomposition for individual fungi and two selected pairs. Inputs: t, I_c, S. Outputs: D.
MU-A-2021-2110178-008: Represent one fungal population under a dry-weight capacity. Inputs: r, n, t. Outputs: x.
MU-A-2021-2110178-009: Represent pairwise fungal competition through resource-equivalent cross terms. Inputs: r_1, r_2, n_1, n_2, s_1, s_2, t. Outputs: x, y.
MU-A-2021-2110178-010: Compare three fungal pairs over the short resource-rich horizon. Inputs: t, r. Outputs: x, y.
MU-A-2021-2110178-011: Compare exclusion and coexistence under long-run resource competition. Inputs: t, s. Outputs: x, y.
MU-A-2021-2110178-012: Map temperature to species growth rates before the declared drop line. Inputs: T. Outputs: G_WR, G_BR, G_AN.
MU-A-2021-2110178-013: Simulate two fungal pairs at 10, 20, and 30 degrees C. Inputs: T, t. Outputs: x, y.
MU-A-2021-2110178-014: Translate temperature-driven growth changes into single and pair lignin decomposition rates. Inputs: T. Outputs: D.
MU-A-2021-2110178-015: Translate ambient humidity through tolerance, growth, competitiveness, and decomposition. Inputs: H. Outputs: D.
MU-A-2021-2110178-016: Relate atmospheric change to temperature, precipitation, drought, and dominant-species selection. Inputs: A_trend. Outputs: S_dom.
MU-A-2021-2110178-017: Rank single species and persistent pairs for selected temperature and humidity regimes. Inputs: E, T, H. Outputs: D_WR, D_BR, D_WA, D_BA, R.
MU-A-2021-2110178-018: Explain how community variety may support decomposition efficiency and recovery under environmental change. Inputs: B, V. Outputs: Eff, Res.

The BR-Aspergillus scenario also retains both states under the assigned coexistence setting.

Brown-rot and its Aspergillus pair rank higher under the paper's low-humidity interpretation.
White-rot and its Aspergillus pair rank higher under the paper's high-humidity interpretation.
The paper expects stronger environmental variation to accelerate selection among fungal types.
The table shows all four alternatives near 5 percent and marks no advantaged species.

task_reconstruction.decision: Use the paper's conditional comparison structure while withholding uncalibrated regional, persistence, diversity, and resilience claims from reusable rules.
task_reconstruction.objective: Model multi-species fungal decomposition in a fixed patch, characterize short/long interactions under environmental variation, rank persistent species and combinations across named environments, and explain biodiversity effects.

verification.summary: The negative OLS direction is an internal association check for the trade-off; it cannot establish predictive validity without coefficients, residuals, uncertainty, or holdout data.
The rise-then-plateau shape checks qualitative plausibility of the kinetic output, but no empirical decomposition trajectory is compared.
Restoring competition changes the trajectory class across horizons as intended; because s encodes outcome class, the comparison checks implementation logic rather than prediction.
Aligned one-factor panels expose directional response and timing changes; they do not quantify global sensitivity or response-law uncertainty.
The low/high reversal is a mechanism plausibility check; no independent data validate the crossover or pair shift.
The tables put inputs, outputs, and rankings together, enabling consistency checks, but their percentages do not reproduce from reported equations.
The authors' four strengths are self-assessments over internal scenarios; the evidence does not include external field validation, uncertainty, or code reproduction.
The two-page article preserves most of the technical route, but audience simplification must not upgrade qualitative conclusions into established ecological facts.

visualization_observations.summary: Analytical purpose: three-image species orientation. Three labeled microscopy/image panels identify white-rot, brown-rot, and Aspergillus before modeling; it supports object recognition, not parameter estimation. Construction: three cited images with letter labels and one shared caption. Boundary/accessibility: source quality and color are nonessential, but species names must remain readable.

Analytical purpose: model architecture and handoff. A flowchart routes single-fungus decomposition and population interaction branches into environmental forcing and final decomposition change. Construction: labeled boxes, directional arrows, and Model I-III braces. Boundary/accessibility: arrows need typed variable/unit contracts; small text and pale lines reduce legibility.

Analytical purpose: symbol ledger. A compact table defines kinetic, trait, environmental, growth, and competition symbols before equations. Construction: symbol/definition rows. Boundary/accessibility: units are incomplete for several symbols, so the table is orientation rather than dimensional closure.

Analytical purpose: biochemical mechanism. The unnumbered A+E0 -> E0A -> E0+P chain precedes Michaelis-Menten kinetics and explains catalytic regeneration. Construction: centered reaction arrows. Boundary/accessibility: symbols require the adjacent prose definitions and should not be inferred from the image alone.

Analytical purpose: trait-fit direction. A scatterplot with one OLS line shows a negative association between the paper's moisture-tolerance index and decomposition-rate index. Encodings: index axes roughly 0.1-0.9 and 0.4-0.85, open markers, solid fit line. Boundary: no uncertainty band, residuals, coefficient, sample provenance, or growth-tolerance fit is shown.

Analytical purpose: species competitiveness lookup. Three columns align white-rot, brown-rot, and Aspergillus with I_c values 0.015, 0.009, and 0.021. Purpose: provide model-ready coefficients. Boundary: growth source, units, transformation, and uncertainty are missing.

Analytical purpose: single-versus-pair decomposition curves. Two panels compare cellulose and lignin decomposition-rate trajectories for singles and selected pairs. Encodings: time on x without units, percent-like rate on y, labeled black curves. Claim: one pair is synergistic and one competitive. Boundary: curve construction and uncertainty are not reproducible.

Analytical purpose: shared scenario parameters. A matrix aligns initial/maximum dry weight, growth rate, optimum temperature range, and optimum humidity for three fungi. Purpose: initialize pair simulations and environmental response lines. Boundary: growth-rate units and exact sources are absent; later temperature prose conflicts with the table.

Analytical purpose: short-horizon pair small multiples. Three aligned 0-7 day panels compare dry-weight growth for all pairs under the no-competition assumption. Encodings: color-coded species lines, g on y, days on x. Claim: growth is nearly independent and rate-driven. Boundary: this is an assumption-controlled baseline, not observed interaction evidence.

Analytical purpose: long-horizon exclusion/coexistence small multiples. Three aligned 0-500 day panels show one exclusion case and two coexistence-like cases. Encodings match Figure 5. Purpose: contrast resource-limited dynamics. Boundary: coefficients 2 or 0.5 encode the outcome class and no equilibrium diagnostics or uncertainty are shown.

Analytical purpose: temperature-growth response construction. A conceptual rise-optimum-drop sketch is paired with three species lines and red drop markers. Encodings: degree C on x and g/day on y; formulas 0.0015625T, 0.0009615T, and 0.001825T. Boundary: legend colors, drop locations, Table 3 ranges, and prose thresholds are inconsistent.

Analytical purpose: white-rot/brown-rot temperature sweep. Three 1000-day panels at 10, 20, and 30 C show faster dominance and decline as assumed temperature response changes. Annotations explain the intended mechanism. Boundary: panel horizon differs from the earlier 500-day definition and a zero growth-rate annotation does not imply immediate zero biomass.

Analytical purpose: brown-rot/Aspergillus temperature sweep. Three aligned panels reuse the temperature experiment for a complementary-resource pair. Purpose: compare direct temperature effects with synergy. Boundary: the figure annotation and prose disagree about which species has zero growth at 30 C.

Analytical purpose: temperature interface chain. Four rounded boxes show T -> growth u -> competitiveness I_c -> decomposition D. Purpose: expose model handoffs. Boundary: no equations, units, or uncertainty are printed on the arrows; blue boxes alone are not quantitative coupling.

Analytical purpose: temperature decomposition comparison. Two panels compare single fungi and Aspergillus-added pairs over temperature, with peak and shift annotations. Purpose: show level and optimum-location changes. Boundary: hand-drawn curves lack construction details, axes lack full calibration, and pair uplift is not equation-backed.

Analytical purpose: humidity interface chain. Five boxes show H -> tolerance m -> growth u -> competitiveness I_c -> decomposition D. Purpose: reveal the extra trait mediator. Boundary: environmental H and species trait m are conceptually distinct, yet the mapping is not specified.

Analytical purpose: humidity decomposition comparison. Two panels compare single and paired decomposition across a 0-100 percent humidity axis and annotate low/high ranking shifts. Boundary: crossover values, response equations, and pair construction are absent; colors and thin lines need redundant labels.

Analytical purpose: atmospheric-trend causal diagram. A vertical/branched flow links atmospheric change and carbon dioxide increase to temperature fluctuation, high temperature, uneven precipitation, drought, and dominant-species selection. Purpose: communicate a qualitative causal story. Boundary: arrows are not a quantified climate model.

Analytical purpose: representative environment map. A world map labels Washington, Sahara, Gansu, and Congo Basin with selected temperatures or humidity. Purpose: make scenario inputs tangible. Boundary: map source, temporal averaging, spatial representativeness, and uncertainty are not provided; text inside callouts is small.

Analytical purpose: temperature decision table. Rows for cold temperate, warm temperate, and tropical rainforest align temperature, four decomposition percentages, and advantaged/disadvantaged choices. Purpose: translate curves to decisions. Boundary: cold-row tie conflicts with prose; time horizon and derivation are missing.

Analytical purpose: humidity decision table. Rows for arid, semi-arid, and tropical rainforest align humidity, four decomposition percentages, and choices. Purpose: mirror Figure 16 for a second input. Boundary: ranges are collapsed to undisclosed calculation points and the percentages are unreproducible.

Analytical purpose: public carbon-cycle orientation. A cited ecosystem diagram gives introductory readers a visual location for fungi in the carbon cycle. Purpose: mechanism orientation, not paper-specific evidence. Boundary: third-party labels and image credit are excluded from positive author-language evidence.

Analytical purpose: public forest-mycorrhiza orientation. A large cited forest/root illustration anchors the biodiversity section in a recognizable ecosystem. Purpose: communicate ecological context. Boundary: the visual includes categories not modeled in the technical solution and cannot validate its pairwise results.

Analytical purpose: audience-layered communication layout. Pages 22-23 use a title/deck, drop caps, numbered sections, two-column text, two contextual figures, and short mechanism/result blocks. Purpose: satisfy the textbook contract while preserving the technical evidence order. Boundary: decorative hierarchy must not hide conditions or contradict the technical tables.

weaknesses.summary: V_E is called the initial speed while multiplying both enzyme and substrate concentrations; its unit and catalytic interpretation are not defined, so dimensional closure cannot be checked.
The printed initial enzyme condition appears as CE_0=aP_0 although the state is E; the notation is ambiguous and is preserved rather than silently repaired.

The negative sign before k_d times the concentration bracket appears inconsistent with integrating equations 3-4 from C_0 to a smaller C, and can yield a negative elapsed time under ordinary positive parameters.
k_d is introduced as a first-order rate coefficient but is redefined as a competitiveness index without a unit conversion or explanation of how a dimensionless trait index occupies the 1/time slot.
Equation 7 makes competitiveness a function of u and m, but the reported final equation 8 drops m even though the prose says moisture tolerance modifies the growth-only index.

The displayed OLS plot relates moisture tolerance to decomposition, not growth to moisture tolerance; the intermediate m=g(u) relation, coefficient table, residuals, sample provenance, and uncertainty are missing.

The coefficient 0.00176 has no stated units, intercept rationale, fit statistic, confidence interval, or domain, and Table 2's downstream values cannot be independently reproduced from cited growth inputs.
No displayed equation maps individual kinetic parameters into the pair curves, the time axis has no unit, and the claimed synergistic and inhibitory percentage levels are not calibrated or validated.
Initial/maximum dry weights, growth rates, optimum temperatures, and humidity values have no source citations; growth-rate units are absent and later temperature claims contradict the table.
The printed effect of x on y uses x/n_2, whereas x's own capacity is n_1 in equation 10; the denominator asymmetry is not explained.
The prose defines x and y as population numbers, Table 3 and every trajectory use dry weight in grams, and no conversion between individuals and biomass is supplied.

The paper sets s_1=s_2=2 when elimination is assumed and 0.5 when coexistence is assumed, then presents the resulting elimination/coexistence as a model conclusion; this is circular scenario construction rather than prediction.
The short-run analysis removes competition by assumption, so the statement that combinations have no effect cannot answer whether the species biologically interact over seven days.
Long term is defined as 500 days in the Summary and Figure 6, but temperature interaction panels run to 1000 days without explaining the changed horizon.

Figure 7's legend, line slopes, and red drop locations do not reconcile with Table 3: Aspergillus is listed as optimal at 20-25 C but later treated as the high-temperature species, while white-rot's line extends to 40 C.
Growth is forced to rise linearly from zero and then drop abruptly to zero after a maximum without species data, decline equations, threshold calibration, or uncertainty.

The text says brown-rot growth rate is zero, but the plotted brown-rot biomass remains positive and decays gradually; zero derivative, zero intrinsic growth, and zero population are not distinguished.
The figure annotation says Aspergillus growth rate is zero while the prose says brown-rot is zero and Aspergillus grows rapidly; the identity of the thresholded species is internally contradictory.
The temperature-to-decomposition arrows have no equations for pair uplift or optimum shift, so the plotted combination curves and annotations cannot be reconstructed from Models I-II.
The paper supplies no ambient-humidity-to-tolerance or tolerance-to-growth equation, yet reports quantitative decomposition curves and crossover behavior.

The official moisture-tolerance trait is a scaled competitive-ranking/niche-width difference, but the paper treats it as resistance to ambient relative humidity and uses optimum humidity percentages without a calibrated bridge.

Atmospheric carbon dioxide, temperature fluctuation, precipitation, drought, and selection are connected only by qualitative arrows; no atmospheric trend data, time scale, spatial support, or response model enters the calculations.
The official arboreal environment requirement is never modeled or given an explicit disposition; temperate, arid, semi-arid, and tropical cases do not cover that missing deliverable.
The prose names brown-rot and BR-Aspergillus as dominant at 7 C, but Figure 16 reports all four alternatives at about 5 percent, no advantaged species, and all disadvantaged.
The scenario percentages have no equation trace, time horizon, code, uncertainty, or definition of whether decomposition rate means instantaneous rate or cumulative percent mass loss.
The semi-arid text gives a 20-60 percent range but the table uses 60 percent; other regimes use inequalities or ranges without a sampling rule, sensitivity band, or cited averaging period.

No diversity metric, richness/evenness level, community larger than a pair, or community-wide decomposition calculation supports the statement that more diversity makes decomposition faster and more complete.
No perturbation, recovery trajectory, resilience variable, baseline, or acceptance threshold supports the claim that diversity makes the environment recover better and faster.

Three temperature scenarios and qualitative humidity curves are called sensitivity analysis and used to claim stability, but no sensitivity index, joint uncertainty, parameter interaction, recommendation reversal, or stability criterion is reported.

Several citations do not match the claims they are attached to: climate, regional temperature/humidity, and decomposition-mechanism statements resolve to composting, lignin, dye-wastewater, trait-trade-off, or kinetics references rather than the asserted facts.
The article says it analyzes a large number of fungi and environmental factors, while the technical model selects three fungi and two factors with unsourced parameters.

The article says low and high temperate temperatures keep the same dominant species because temperature impact is small, conflicting with the technical section's strong temperature-sensitivity and threshold narrative.
